title: 🎢 Forces & Motion Park
description: Welcome to the Forces & Motion Park! You are a Grade 6 student who has been chosen to help redesign the school's adventure playground using real physics. Over 14 weeks, you will learn about pushes, pulls, gravity, friction, and simple machines — then use that knowledge to design rides, ramps, and contraptions. Experiment with ramps, pulleys, levers, and pendulums while keeping your designs safe and your ideas bold. Can you become the Master Engineer and build the ultimate Rube Goldberg machine for the Physics Showcase?
subject: physics
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student exploring forces and motion over a 14-week physics lab program.
Each week presents a physics challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, safety, and engineering skill.
Watch your dashboard — your Workshop Stations (Force Lab, Motion Track, Machine Shop, Test Range, Design Studio) are interconnected.
NPCs like Coach Newton (teacher), Gizmo (engineering mascot), Priya, and Sam react to your decisions.
Random events like broken equipment and visiting engineers will test your adaptability.
Keep your Safety Rating high — if it drops too low, you will be banned from the test range!
learning_objectives: Understand forces as pushes and pulls that can change an object's motion
Learn about gravity and how it affects all objects on Earth
Explore friction — what causes it and how it helps and hinders motion
Discover Newton's Laws of Motion through hands-on experiments
Understand how simple machines (levers, pulleys, inclined planes) multiply force
Design and build mechanical systems that apply physics principles
cultural_context: School physics laboratory, hands-on STEM learning, engineering design challenges

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Forces Fundamentals

questions.question: What is the unit used to measure force?

choices.text: Newton (N)
Kilogram (kg)
Meter per second (m/s)

questions.explanation: Force is measured in Newtons (N), named after Sir Isaac Newton. Kilograms measure mass, and meters per second measure speed.

questions.question: What is the main difference between mass and weight?

choices.text: There is no difference — they mean the same thing
Mass is the amount of matter in an object and stays the same everywhere, but weight changes with gravity
Weight stays the same everywhere, but mass depends on gravity

questions.explanation: Mass (measured in kg) is the amount of matter and never changes. Weight (measured in Newtons) is the gravitational force on that mass and changes depending on where you are — for example, you weigh less on the Moon because its gravity is weaker.

questions.question: A book is sitting still on a table. Which statement about forces is correct?

choices.text: No forces are acting on the book since it is not moving
Only gravity is acting on the book
Gravity pulls the book down and the table pushes it up — these balanced forces keep it still

questions.explanation: Even a stationary object has forces acting on it. Gravity pulls the book downward, while the table exerts an upward normal force. These two forces are equal and opposite (balanced), so the book stays at rest.

questions.question: If you dropped a hammer and a feather in a vacuum (no air), what would happen?

choices.text: The hammer would hit the ground first because it is heavier
They would both hit the ground at the same time
The feather would hit the ground first because it is lighter

questions.explanation: Without air resistance, gravity accelerates all objects at the same rate regardless of mass. Galileo proved this centuries ago, and Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott demonstrated it on the Moon in 1971 by dropping a hammer and a feather together.

checkpoints.review_summary: Forces are pushes or pulls that act on objects, measured in Newtons (N). Mass is the amount of matter in an object (measured in kg) and stays constant, while weight is the force of gravity on that mass and changes with location. Gravity is an invisible force that pulls all objects toward Earth and accelerates them equally in the absence of air resistance. Forces act on objects even when they are stationary — balanced forces (equal and opposite) keep objects at rest, while unbalanced forces cause changes in motion.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 2: Motion, Laws & Simple Machines

questions.question: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia) states that an object in motion will:

choices.text: Naturally slow down and stop on its own
Keep moving at the same speed and direction unless an outside force acts on it
Speed up over time because of its inertia

questions.explanation: Newton's First Law says objects resist changes to their motion. A moving object keeps moving at constant speed in a straight line unless a force (like friction or a push) acts on it. On Earth, friction and air resistance are the forces that slow things down — in space, objects coast forever.

questions.question: According to Newton's Second Law (F = m x a), if you push an empty shopping trolley and a full shopping trolley with the same force, which accelerates more?

choices.text: The full trolley accelerates more because it has more mass
Both accelerate equally since the force is the same
The empty trolley accelerates more because it has less mass

questions.explanation: From F = m x a, we get a = F / m. With the same force, a smaller mass produces a larger acceleration. The empty trolley (less mass) speeds up faster than the full one. This is why race cars are built to be lightweight!

questions.question: How does a lever make it easier to lift a heavy object?

choices.text: It creates extra energy to help lift the load
It multiplies your force by trading force for distance — you push with less force over a greater distance
It removes gravity from the heavy object

questions.explanation: A lever is a simple machine that multiplies force. By placing the fulcrum close to the load and pushing on the long end, you use less effort — but you push through a greater distance. Simple machines never create energy; they trade force for distance. The total work (force times distance) stays the same.

questions.question: Why does a longer, gentler ramp require less force to push a heavy box to the top compared to a short, steep ramp?

choices.text: The longer ramp has less friction, so the box slides more easily
The longer ramp spreads the same amount of work over a greater distance, so less force is needed at each point
Gravity does not act on objects on gentle slopes

questions.explanation: An inclined plane (ramp) is a simple machine that trades distance for force. A longer, gentler ramp means you push over a greater distance but with less force at each point. The total work done (lifting the box to the same height) is the same either way — but a gentle ramp makes the task feel much easier. This is why wheelchair ramps use a gradual slope.

checkpoints.review_summary: Newton's First Law tells us objects resist changes to their motion (inertia) — a moving object keeps moving unless a force stops it. Newton's Second Law (F = m x a) shows that more force means more acceleration, and more mass means less acceleration for the same force. Simple machines like levers, pulleys, and inclined planes make work easier by trading force for distance — they multiply your effort but never create new energy. A lever with the fulcrum close to the load lets you lift heavy objects with less force, and a longer, gentler ramp requires less pushing force than a steep one to reach the same height.

rounds.round_title: Week 1: Welcome to the World of Forces
rounds.situation: It is your first day in the physics workshop! The room is filled with ramps, springs, weights, pulleys, toy cars, and track sections. Coach Newton welcomes the class with a big smile: 'Everything that moves or stays still does so because of forces — pushes and pulls! Over the next 14 weeks, you will become force experts and build incredible machines. But first — what IS a force?' He pushes a toy car across the table. 'Let us find out!'
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your forces and motion education.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Spending time on fundamentals now will make every future experiment and build easier and safer.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can you think of five forces that act on you right now as you sit in this chair?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students entering a bright physics workshop for the first time, benches with ramps, pulleys, springs and toy cars, excited faces, Coach Newton pushing a toy car

choices.label: A. A force is a push or pull that can change an object's speed, direction, or shape

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Identifying the precise scientific definition shows you can analyze concepts carefully before jumping to conclusions.

choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A force is any push or pull acting on an object. Forces can make objects start moving, stop moving, speed up, slow down, change direction, or change shape (like squeezing a sponge). Forces are measured in Newtons (N), named after Sir Isaac Newton — the father of modern physics!

choices.label: B. A force is the energy stored inside an object that makes it move on its own

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Confusing force with stored energy shows a common reasoning gap — distinguishing related concepts is key strategic thinking.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Force is NOT energy stored inside an object. Force is a push or pull applied FROM OUTSIDE (or by gravity, magnetism, etc.) that acts ON an object. Energy and force are related but different concepts. An object sitting on a table has no stored force — but forces (gravity pulling down, table pushing up) are still acting on it!

choices.label: C. Forces only exist when objects are moving — stationary objects have no forces on them

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking forces only exist during motion overlooks invisible forces — strategic thinkers consider what they cannot directly see.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Forces act on objects ALL the time, even when they are perfectly still! A book on a table has gravity pulling it down AND the table pushing it up — these balanced forces keep it stationary. If forces only existed during motion, nothing would stay on the ground. You are sitting still right now, but gravity is constantly pulling you down!

choices.label: D. The unit of force is the kilogram (kg)

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Mixing up units of mass and force reveals a need to organize related facts systematically before applying them.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The kilogram (kg) is the unit of MASS, not force. The unit of force is the Newton (N), named after Sir Isaac Newton. Mass tells you how much matter is in an object, while force tells you how hard a push or pull is. On Earth, a 1 kg object has a weight (gravitational force) of about 9.8 Newtons.

rounds.round_title: Week 2: Push & Pull — Forces in Action
rounds.situation: Coach Newton sets up a challenge: 'Forces are just pushes and pulls. But how STRONG are they? How do we MEASURE them?' He hands out spring scales (Newton meters) and asks each team to measure the force needed to drag different objects across the table. 'Can you predict which objects need more force?' Sam is already setting up his data table while Priya is attaching the spring scale to a heavy dictionary.
rounds.goal: Measure forces using spring scales and understand what affects force needed to move objects.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Making predictions BEFORE measuring is the heart of the scientific method. Predict, test, learn!
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does it take more force to push a heavy box than a light one? What if the surface was ice instead of wood?
rounds.image_prompt: Student pulling a brick across a table using a spring scale, reading showing 5 Newtons, another student recording data, lab bench with various objects to test

choices.label: A. Mass is the amount of matter in an object and stays the same everywhere, but weight changes with gravity

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Distinguishing mass from weight requires analyzing how gravity changes the picture — a core scientific reasoning skill.

choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Mass (measured in kg) is the amount of matter in an object — it stays the same whether you are on Earth, the Moon, or floating in space. Weight (measured in Newtons) is the force of gravity pulling on that mass. On the Moon, your mass stays the same but your weight drops to about 1/6th of your Earth weight because the Moon has weaker gravity!

choices.label: B. Weight and mass are the same thing — they both measure how heavy something is

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Treating mass and weight as identical skips a critical distinction that affects every force calculation you will make.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Mass and weight are DIFFERENT! Mass measures how much matter is in an object (in kg) and never changes. Weight is the gravitational force pulling on that mass (in Newtons) and depends on where you are. Your mass is the same on Earth and the Moon, but you weigh about 6 times less on the Moon because its gravity is weaker!

choices.label: C. Heavier objects always fall faster than lighter objects

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Assuming heavier objects fall faster ignores hidden variables like air resistance — strategic thinkers isolate variables.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 In the absence of air resistance, ALL objects fall at the same rate regardless of their mass! Galileo proved this over 400 years ago. A hammer and a feather dropped in a vacuum (no air) hit the ground at the same time. Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott actually demonstrated this on the Moon in 1971. Air resistance is what makes lighter objects seem to fall slower on Earth!

choices.label: D. Gravity only pulls objects downward when they are above the ground

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Limiting gravity to airborne objects misses how forces act constantly — thinking beyond the obvious builds stronger reasoning.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Gravity acts on ALL objects ALL the time — not just when they are in the air! Even when you stand on the ground, gravity is pulling you downward. The ground pushes back up (normal force) to keep you from sinking. If the ground suddenly vanished, you would fall. Gravity also works underground, underwater, and in every direction toward Earth's center!

rounds.situation: Coach Newton holds an apple above the table and lets go. It falls. 'Why does everything fall DOWN and never UP?' he asks with a grin. 'Gravity! The force that keeps us on the ground, keeps the Moon orbiting Earth, and keeps Earth orbiting the Sun.' He sets up drop experiments from different heights. 'Today we investigate gravity — the most universal force in the universe.'
rounds.goal: Understand gravity, how it affects falling objects, and why mass matters.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Gravity works the same everywhere, but its effects surprise us. Being willing to change your thinking when experiments surprise you is real scientific thinking.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time, which would hit the ground first? What if there was no air?
rounds.image_prompt: Student dropping two different sized balls from the same height above a table, another student timing with a stopwatch, Coach Newton watching, apple on the desk

choices.label: A. Friction is a force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact, and it depends on surface roughness

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Connecting friction to surface roughness shows you can link cause and effect in physical systems.

choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Friction is the force that resists the sliding motion of two surfaces against each other. Rougher surfaces create more friction (sandpaper on wood) and smoother surfaces create less (ice on ice). Friction is caused by tiny bumps and ridges on surfaces interlocking with each other. More force pressing surfaces together also increases friction!

choices.label: B. Friction is always harmful and engineers try to eliminate it completely

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Seeing friction as only harmful is one-sided — evaluating both benefits and drawbacks is strategic analysis.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Friction is not always harmful — it is often essential! Without friction, you could not walk (your feet would slip), cars could not brake, and you could not hold a pencil. Friction helps us grip, stop, and control motion. Sometimes we WANT more friction (brake pads, shoe soles) and sometimes LESS (oiling machine parts, ice skating).

choices.label: C. Rolling friction is greater than sliding friction, which is why wheels slow you down

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Comparing rolling vs sliding friction requires analyzing real-world evidence — wheels exist because rolling friction is less.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Rolling friction is actually MUCH LESS than sliding friction — that is exactly WHY wheels are so useful! It is easier to roll a barrel than to drag it across the floor. Ancient Egyptians discovered this when they used log rollers to move heavy stones. Ball bearings in machines use rolling friction to reduce energy loss.

choices.label: D. Friction does not produce any heat — surfaces stay cold when rubbed together

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Denying friction produces heat ignores everyday evidence like warm hands — strategic thinkers test claims against experience.

choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Friction ALWAYS produces heat! Rub your hands together quickly and you will feel them warm up. That is friction converting motion energy into heat energy. This is how early humans started fires by rubbing sticks together. Car brakes get extremely hot from friction, and meteors burn up from friction with the atmosphere!

rounds.round_title: Week 4: Friction — The Force That Grips
rounds.situation: Coach Newton puts on rubber-soled shoes and smooth leather shoes and tries to slide across the floor in each pair. The class laughs as he nearly falls in the leather ones! 'Friction is the force that opposes motion between surfaces,' he explains. 'Sometimes we want MORE friction (like shoe grip) and sometimes LESS (like a waterslide). Today we measure friction and learn to control it!'
rounds.goal: Understand friction, measure it, and learn when it helps and when it hinders.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Honest data collection matters — if your measurements seem wrong, do not change them. Investigate why! Unexpected results often lead to the biggest discoveries.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do car tires have treads? What would happen if tires were completely smooth?
rounds.image_prompt: Student dragging a wooden block across surfaces — sandpaper, glass, carpet — with a spring scale measuring friction force, data table visible, Coach Newton demonstrating shoes

choices.label: A. Gravity and magnetism are non-contact forces because they act without the objects touching each other
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Non-contact forces can act across a distance without the objects physically touching. Gravity pulls you toward Earth even though you are not touching the center of the planet. A magnet attracts iron nails without touching them. Contact forces (like friction, push, and pull) require the objects to touch each other directly.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Gravity is a contact force because the ground is always touching our feet
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Gravity is a NON-CONTACT force! It pulls on you even when you are not touching the ground — like when you jump, or when an apple falls from a tree. The ground touching your feet is the NORMAL force (a contact force). Gravity reaches across space — the Sun's gravity holds Earth in orbit across 150 million kilometers!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Friction is a non-contact force because it seems to slow things down invisibly
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Friction is a CONTACT force because it only acts when two surfaces are physically touching each other. You cannot have friction between objects that are not in contact! Even air resistance (a type of friction) requires air molecules to physically bump into the moving object. No contact = no friction.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Non-contact forces are weaker than contact forces and have no real effect on daily life
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Non-contact forces are incredibly powerful and essential to daily life! Gravity keeps you on the ground, holds the atmosphere around Earth, and keeps planets in orbit. Magnetism powers electric motors in everything from fans to cars. Electrostatic force holds atoms together. Non-contact forces literally hold the universe together!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Coach Newton sets up a long track down the hallway. 'Speed tells us how fast something moves. But acceleration tells us how quickly speed CHANGES,' he explains. 'When you push a shopping trolley, it starts slow and gets faster — that is acceleration. When you brake on a bicycle, you decelerate.' He gives each team a stopwatch, a toy car, and a track. 'Measure speed at different points. Is your car speeding up, slowing down, or staying constant?'
rounds.goal: Understand the difference between speed and acceleration through measurement.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Speed = distance / time. This simple formula unlocks the ability to predict motion. Master it and you master the physics of moving objects!
rounds.reflection_prompt: A car going 60 km/h hits the brakes. What forces cause it to decelerate? How is deceleration different from acceleration?
rounds.image_prompt: Long track in school hallway with toy car rolling, student timing with stopwatch at marked distance intervals, another student recording data, motion blur effect on car

challenge.question: A cart has a mass of 5 kg. If you push it with a force of 10 N, what is its acceleration?

choices.label: A. When balanced forces act on an object, it stays at rest or keeps moving at constant speed
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When all forces on an object cancel out (balanced forces), there is no change in motion. A book on a table stays still because gravity down = normal force up. A car cruising at constant speed has engine force forward = friction + air resistance backward. Unbalanced forces are needed to START, STOP, or CHANGE motion!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. An object can only move if unbalanced forces are acting on it at every moment
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 An object can keep moving even with balanced forces! If you kick a ball in outer space (no friction, no air resistance), it will keep moving forever at constant speed with zero net force. Balanced forces mean no change in motion — an already-moving object keeps moving at the same speed. You only need unbalanced forces to CHANGE motion.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. If two people push a box with equal force from the same side, the forces are balanced
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 If both people push from the SAME side, their forces ADD up — this is an UNBALANCED force, and the box will accelerate in that direction! Forces are only balanced when they are EQUAL in size but OPPOSITE in direction. For balanced forces, the two people would need to push with equal force from OPPOSITE sides.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. A falling skydiver is always experiencing unbalanced forces throughout the entire fall
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Initially, the skydiver accelerates because gravity (down) is greater than air resistance (up) — unbalanced forces. But as speed increases, air resistance grows until it EQUALS gravity. At that point, forces are BALANCED and the skydiver falls at a constant speed called terminal velocity — about 200 km/h!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Coach Newton sets a book on the table. 'This book is not moving. But forces ARE acting on it — gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up. These forces are BALANCED, so nothing moves.' He then pushes the book and it slides. 'Now the forces are UNBALANCED — my push overcame friction. Unbalanced forces cause acceleration!' He sets up a tug-of-war rope between two spring scales. 'Explore balance and imbalance!'
rounds.goal: Understand the difference between balanced and unbalanced forces and their effects on motion.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Great designs balance forces deliberately. A bridge, a chair, a bicycle — all work because engineers carefully balanced the forces acting on them.
rounds.reflection_prompt: A skydiver falls at constant speed (terminal velocity). Are the forces on them balanced or unbalanced? Explain your reasoning.
rounds.image_prompt: Two students having a tug-of-war with spring scales attached to a rope, force readings visible, Coach Newton drawing force diagrams on whiteboard, balanced arrows

choices.label: A. Newton's First Law says an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving, unless an outside force acts on it
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ This is also called the Law of Inertia. Inertia is an object's resistance to change in motion. A ball on the floor stays still until kicked (resists starting). A hockey puck on ice keeps sliding until friction stops it (resists stopping). The more massive an object, the more inertia it has — that is why a truck is harder to push than a bicycle!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Objects naturally slow down and stop on their own, even without any forces acting on them
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 This is one of the biggest misconceptions in physics! Objects do NOT naturally slow down on their own. On Earth, friction and air resistance (forces!) slow things down. In space, where there is almost no friction, objects keep moving forever at the same speed. A spacecraft can travel for millions of years without slowing down!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. A heavier object needs less force to start moving because it has more inertia
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 More inertia means an object is HARDER to start moving, stop, or change direction — not easier! A loaded truck (more mass, more inertia) needs a much bigger force to start moving than an empty one. That is why big ships take kilometers to stop — their massive inertia resists the change from moving to still.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Seatbelts in cars are not related to Newton's First Law
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Seatbelts are a PERFECT example of Newton's First Law! When a car stops suddenly in a crash, your body wants to keep moving forward (inertia). Without a seatbelt, you would fly forward into the dashboard or windshield. The seatbelt provides the unbalanced force needed to stop YOUR motion along with the car. Seatbelts save lives because of inertia!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

challenge.question: A 3 kg ball is pushed with a force of 12 N. What is its acceleration?

widget_answer.prompt: A 3kg object accelerates at 2 m/s². What is the net force?

rounds.round_title: Week 7: The Roller Coaster Gets Stuck!
rounds.situation: CRISIS! The class has been building a marble roller coaster for weeks — a long track with loops, hills, and jumps. Today, during the big test run, the marble stops halfway through the first loop! It does not have enough speed to complete the loop and falls off the track. The entire design has failed. Coach Newton stays calm: 'In engineering, failure is just data. What went wrong, and how do we fix it?' The class is disappointed but ready to troubleshoot.
rounds.goal: Diagnose why the roller coaster failed and redesign it using physics principles.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Every great engineer has faced failures. The Wright Brothers crashed their planes dozens of times before flying. Failure is the price of innovation.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does a roller coaster need to start from a height HIGHER than its tallest loop? What physics principle explains this?
rounds.image_prompt: Marble roller coaster track with a marble stuck at the top of a loop, students looking disappointed but thinking, Coach Newton at whiteboard drawing energy diagrams, workshop setting

choices.label: A. Speed is calculated by dividing distance by time: Speed = Distance / Time
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The formula Speed = Distance / Time tells us how fast something is moving. If a car travels 100 km in 2 hours, its average speed is 100/2 = 50 km/h. You can rearrange this formula: Distance = Speed x Time, or Time = Distance / Speed. This simple formula is one of the most useful equations in all of physics!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Speed is calculated by multiplying distance by time: Speed = Distance x Time
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Speed = Distance DIVIDED by Time, not multiplied! Think about it: if you walk 10 km in 2 hours, your speed is 10/2 = 5 km/h. If you multiplied (10 x 2 = 20), the answer would not make sense — you would get faster just by taking longer! Distance = Speed x Time is correct for finding distance, but Speed = Distance / Time.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. A car traveling at 60 km/h will cover 30 km in 2 hours
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Using Distance = Speed x Time: 60 km/h x 2 hours = 120 km, not 30 km. The car covers 60 km every hour, so in 2 hours it covers 120 km. You might have divided instead of multiplied. Remember: to find distance, MULTIPLY speed by time. To find speed, DIVIDE distance by time.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Two objects with the same speed always reach the finish line at the same time
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Having the same speed does not mean finishing at the same time — it depends on WHEN they started and what DIRECTION they are going! If one car starts 5 minutes later, it arrives later. Also, speed does not include direction. Two cars at 50 km/h going in opposite directions get farther apart, not closer. Velocity includes direction; speed does not.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Coach Newton places a heavy box on the floor. 'Can anyone lift this with one finger?' he challenges. Nobody can — it is too heavy. Then he places a long plank over a brick (a lever and fulcrum) and puts one end under the box. With a gentle push on the other end... the box rises! 'Levers multiply your force!' he announces. 'Archimedes said: Give me a long enough lever and I can move the Earth!'
rounds.goal: Understand how levers work, identify the three classes, and build lever-based machines.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Simple machines do not create energy — they trade force for distance. Understanding this trade-off is key to all mechanical engineering.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Name three levers you use every day. Where is the fulcrum, effort, and load in each?
rounds.image_prompt: Student using a long plank as a lever balanced on a brick fulcrum to lift a heavy box, another student measuring distances, Coach Newton watching with crossed arms and a smile

challenge.question: A lever has its fulcrum 0.5 m from a 20 kg load. You push down 2 m from the fulcrum. What effort force (in N) do you need? (Use g = 10 m/s²)
challenge.formula_hint: Effort × effort arm = Load × load arm. Load force = mass × g

choices.label: A. A lever multiplies force — placing the fulcrum closer to the load means you need less effort to lift it
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A lever is a rigid bar that rotates around a fixed point called the fulcrum. When the fulcrum is closer to the load (heavy object), the effort arm is longer, so you need LESS force to lift the load — but you push through a greater distance. This is called mechanical advantage. Seesaws, crowbars, and scissors are all levers!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Simple machines create extra energy, which is why they make work easier
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Simple machines NEVER create extra energy — energy cannot be created or destroyed (Law of Conservation of Energy). Instead, they trade force for distance. A lever lets you use LESS force, but you must push over a GREATER distance. The total work (force x distance) stays the same! They make tasks easier, not effortless.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. There is only one type of lever — the seesaw type where the fulcrum is in the middle
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 There are THREE classes of levers! Class 1: fulcrum in the middle (seesaw, scissors). Class 2: load in the middle (wheelbarrow, bottle opener). Class 3: effort in the middle (tweezers, fishing rod, your forearm!). Each class has the fulcrum, effort, and load in a different arrangement.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Moving the fulcrum farther from the load makes it easier to lift the load
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Moving the fulcrum FARTHER from the load actually makes it HARDER to lift, not easier! You want the fulcrum CLOSE to the load and your effort arm to be long. Think of using a crowbar to pry open a crate — you place the fulcrum near the lid (load) and push on the long end. The lever equation is: Effort x Effort Distance = Load x Load Distance.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.round_title: Week 9: Pulleys & Gears — Changing Direction and Force
rounds.situation: Coach Newton hangs a pulley from a stand and threads a rope through it. 'Pull down on this rope,' he says. When you pull down, the weight on the other end goes UP! 'Pulleys change the direction of force. Add more pulleys and you can multiply your force too!' He also shows a set of interlocking gears. 'Gears transfer force between shafts and change speed. Bicycles, clocks, and car engines all use gears.'
rounds.goal: Understand how pulleys and gears work to change force direction and magnitude.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Pulleys and gears are building blocks. The more you understand them, the more complex machines you can imagine and build.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does a compound pulley (multiple wheels) make it easier to lift heavy objects? What is the trade-off?
rounds.image_prompt: Student pulling rope through a double pulley system to lift a heavy weight, another student examining interlocking gears, workshop with mechanical components visible

choices.label: A. Pressure equals force divided by area — the same force on a smaller area creates more pressure
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Pressure = Force / Area. When you concentrate the same force on a smaller area, pressure increases dramatically. That is why a sharp knife cuts easily (tiny edge area = high pressure) but a blunt knife does not. A person in high heels exerts more pressure on the floor than an elephant, because the heel area is so tiny!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Pressure increases when the area of contact increases
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Pressure DECREASES when area increases (for the same force). Since Pressure = Force / Area, dividing by a LARGER area gives a SMALLER pressure. That is why snowshoes have large flat surfaces — they spread your weight over a bigger area to reduce pressure and stop you from sinking into snow. Wider tires on trucks work the same way!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. A nail goes into wood easily because it has a large, flat head that pushes the wood
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A nail goes into wood because of its SHARP POINT, not its flat head! The sharp point has a tiny area, which means the same hammer force creates enormous pressure at the tip — enough to push into wood. The flat head is there so the hammer hits it easily without slipping. Small area = high pressure = nail penetrates!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Pressure and force are the same thing and are measured in the same units
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Pressure and force are related but DIFFERENT. Force is measured in Newtons (N) and pressure is measured in Pascals (Pa) or N/m². A 100 N force can create very different pressures depending on the area. Spread over 1 m², it is 100 Pa (gentle). Concentrated on 0.001 m² (like a pin), it is 100,000 Pa (piercing)!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

widget_answer.prompt: Calculate the effort force for a lever (load=200N, load_arm=1m, effort_arm=2m)

rounds.round_title: Week 10: Inclined Planes — Ramps to the Rescue
rounds.situation: Coach Newton asks: 'Would you rather carry a heavy box straight up a cliff, or push it up a long gentle ramp?' Everyone chooses the ramp! 'An inclined plane (ramp) is a simple machine that trades distance for force,' he explains. 'The longer the ramp, the less force you need — but you push over a greater distance. Ancient Egyptians used ramps to build the pyramids!' He sets out ramps of different angles and heavy blocks.
rounds.goal: Understand how inclined planes reduce force and calculate the mechanical advantage of ramps.
rounds.coaching_moment: Risk tolerance: Testing different ramp angles means some will fail. The willingness to try angles that might not work is what leads to discovering the optimal design.
rounds.reflection_prompt: The pyramids were built using ramps. If a pyramid is 150 meters tall, why would a 1-kilometer ramp be easier than a 200-meter ramp?
rounds.image_prompt: Student pushing a heavy block up a wooden ramp with a spring scale measuring force, different angle ramps set up side by side, force comparison chart on whiteboard

choices.label: A. A spring stretches more when a greater force is applied, and returns to its original shape when the force is removed
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ This is described by Hooke's Law: the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied (up to the elastic limit). Double the force = double the stretch. When you release the force, the spring bounces back to its original length. This elastic property makes springs useful in everything from pens to car suspensions to trampolines!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. All materials are elastic — every object returns to its original shape after being stretched
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Only some materials are elastic (springs, rubber bands, steel). Many materials are PLASTIC — they stay deformed permanently. If you bend a paperclip, it does not spring back. Even elastic materials have an 'elastic limit' — stretch them too far and they deform permanently or break. That is why overstretching a spring ruins it!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. A stiffer spring needs less force to stretch it the same distance as a soft spring
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A STIFFER spring needs MORE force to stretch it the same distance — that is what 'stiff' means! In Hooke's Law (F = k x extension), k is the spring constant. A stiffer spring has a higher k value, meaning more force is needed for the same stretch. Car suspension springs are much stiffer than pen springs because they need to support heavy loads.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Spring scales (Newton meters) measure the mass of an object, not the force
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Spring scales (Newton meters) measure FORCE, not mass! They work by measuring how much a spring stretches under a force — the more force, the more the spring extends, and the higher the reading. Since weight is a force (gravity pulling on mass), a spring scale reading changes on different planets. A beam balance measures mass, which stays constant everywhere.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

challenge.question: A lever has effort arm 2m and load arm 0.5m. What is the mechanical advantage?

rounds.round_title: Week 11: Air Resistance — The Invisible Brake
rounds.situation: Coach Newton drops two identical sheets of paper — one flat, one crumpled into a ball. The crumpled one hits the ground first! 'Same mass, same gravity — but different air resistance!' he explains. 'Air resistance is a type of friction that acts on objects moving through air. The bigger the surface area, the more air resistance.' He challenges each team to design the perfect paper airplane AND the perfect parachute.
rounds.goal: Understand air resistance, how it affects falling and flying objects, and how to control it.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Great teams leverage everyone's strengths. Priya's creativity for airplane design and Sam's measurement skills for parachute timing make the perfect combination.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do sports cars have sleek, streamlined shapes while parachutes are big and wide?
rounds.image_prompt: Student dropping a flat piece of paper and a crumpled paper ball simultaneously from a height, one falling slowly, one fast, another student testing paper airplanes

challenge.question: A skydiver with mass 80 kg reaches terminal velocity. At terminal velocity, what is the air resistance force acting on them? (Use g = 10 m/s²)
challenge.formula_hint: At terminal velocity, air resistance = weight = mass × g

choices.label: A. A longer, gentler ramp requires less force to push an object up, but you must push it over a greater distance
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ An inclined plane (ramp) trades force for distance. A gentle 10-meter ramp to reach a 1-meter height needs much less pushing force than lifting straight up, but you travel 10 meters instead of 1. The Ancient Egyptians used ramps kilometers long to move massive stone blocks up to build the pyramids — same principle!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. A steeper ramp is easier to push objects up because gravity helps more on steep slopes
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A steeper ramp is HARDER to push objects up, not easier! On a steeper slope, a larger component of gravity pulls the object back down the ramp. The steepest 'ramp' — straight up at 90 degrees — means lifting the full weight! Gentle slopes give the most mechanical advantage, which is why wheelchair ramps use a gradual 1:12 slope.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. A single fixed pulley doubles the force you can apply to lift an object
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A single FIXED pulley does NOT multiply force at all — it only changes the DIRECTION of the force. You pull down on the rope and the load goes up, but the force needed is the same as lifting directly. To actually multiply force, you need a COMPOUND pulley system (fixed + movable pulleys). A two-pulley system halves the effort but doubles the rope distance.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Screws and wedges are not simple machines — only levers, pulleys, and ramps count
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 There are SIX classical simple machines: lever, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw, and wheel-and-axle. A screw is actually an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder (look at the spiral thread!). A wedge is two inclined planes pushed together (like an axe blade). Every complex machine is a combination of these six basics!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! The class has been building a model bridge for the Physics Showcase — a beautiful truss bridge designed to hold 5 kg. During today's final load test, it collapses at only 3 kg! The carefully built structure buckles, bends, and fails catastrophically. Materials are wasted, the team is devastated, and the Showcase is just two weeks away. Coach Newton examines the wreckage: 'Every bridge failure teaches engineers something. The question is — what did THIS failure teach us?'
rounds.goal: Analyze why the bridge failed and rebuild a stronger design using physics principles.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Real bridges have collapsed throughout history — the Tacoma Narrows, the Tay Bridge. Each failure led to safer designs. Your failure is your greatest teacher.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the difference between a bridge that fails gradually (bends slowly) and one that fails suddenly (snaps)? Which is safer and why?
rounds.image_prompt: Collapsed model bridge on a lab table with broken popsicle sticks and fallen weights, students examining the failure point, Coach Newton sketching a stronger design on whiteboard

choices.label: A. A greater force on the same object produces a greater acceleration (F = mass x acceleration)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Newton's Second Law (F = m x a) tells us that force, mass, and acceleration are linked. Push harder on a shopping trolley (more force) = it speeds up faster (more acceleration). Push the same force on a heavier trolley = it speeds up slower (less acceleration). This formula lets engineers calculate exactly how much force rockets need to launch into space!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. A heavier object accelerates faster than a lighter one when the same force is applied
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 From F = m x a, we get a = F/m. A HEAVIER object (larger m) with the same force (F) produces LESS acceleration (smaller a). Push an empty shopping trolley and a full one with the same force — the empty one speeds up faster! That is why race cars are designed to be lightweight — less mass means more acceleration from the same engine force.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. An object with no force acting on it will automatically decelerate and stop
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 If no net force acts on an object, its acceleration is ZERO (from F = m x a, if F = 0, then a = 0). This means it continues at the SAME speed forever! Objects on Earth slow down because of friction and air resistance (forces!), not because motion naturally stops. In space, with virtually no friction, objects coast forever.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. The acceleration of an object does not depend on its mass — only on the force applied
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Acceleration depends on BOTH force AND mass! From a = F/m, acceleration increases with more force but decreases with more mass. A tennis ball and a bowling ball hit with the same bat force accelerate very differently — the lighter tennis ball zooms away while the heavy bowling ball barely moves. Both force and mass matter equally!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: One week before the Physics Showcase! Coach Newton gives the ultimate challenge: 'Build a Rube Goldberg machine — a chain reaction device that uses at least 5 simple machines to accomplish a simple task in the most complicated way possible! Use ramps, levers, pulleys, dominoes, balls, and anything else you can think of. The more creative, the better!' Priya's eyes light up. Sam starts planning the sequence. This is the culmination of everything you have learned!
rounds.goal: Design and build a Rube Goldberg machine that combines multiple physics principles.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: A Rube Goldberg machine is the ultimate creative engineering challenge — combining everything you know into one spectacular chain reaction.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the most surprising thing you learned about forces this semester? How did you use it in your Rube Goldberg machine?
rounds.image_prompt: Elaborate Rube Goldberg machine on a workshop table with dominoes, ramps, pulleys, lever arms, rolling balls, and a bell at the end, students building and testing sections

choices.label: A. Newton's Third Law: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction — forces always come in pairs
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force in the opposite direction. When a rocket pushes hot gas downward, the gas pushes the rocket upward. When you walk, your foot pushes backward on the ground, and the ground pushes forward on your foot. Forces ALWAYS come in equal and opposite pairs — no exceptions!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. The action force is always stronger than the reaction force
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The action and reaction forces are ALWAYS exactly equal in strength and opposite in direction. When you push a wall with 50 N, the wall pushes you with exactly 50 N. It might SEEM like the action is stronger (you pushed first), but physics does not care who pushed first — both forces are always perfectly matched!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. When a ball hits a window and breaks it, the ball exerts more force on the window than the window exerts on the ball
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Even when a ball breaks a window, the forces are EQUAL! The ball pushes the window with the same force that the window pushes back on the ball. The window breaks because glass is fragile (low breaking strength), not because it received more force. The ball also changes its motion (slows down or bounces) because of the window's equal reaction force on it.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Action-reaction pairs cancel each other out, so nothing should ever be able to move
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Action-reaction forces act on DIFFERENT objects, so they do NOT cancel out! When you push a skateboard backward with your foot (action on skateboard), the skateboard pushes your foot forward (reaction on you). The forces are on two separate objects. Forces only cancel when they act on the SAME object (like balanced forces).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Physics Showcase day is here! The gym is transformed into an engineering exhibition — bridges, roller coasters, catapults, pulley systems, and Rube Goldberg machines fill the space. Parents, teachers, younger students, and a local newspaper reporter are visiting. Your machine is set up and ready. Coach Newton says: 'This is your moment to show the world that physics is not just equations — it is the science of everything that moves!' How will you present?
rounds.goal: Present your physics project at the Showcase and make the most of the experience.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Public demonstration takes courage. Machines might jam, bridges might wobble — but sharing your work with confidence is itself a huge achievement.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, what would you tell your past self about forces and motion? How much have you grown as a scientist and engineer?
rounds.image_prompt: School Physics Showcase in a gymnasium, Rube Goldberg machines and model bridges on display, parents watching demonstrations, students presenting proudly, trophy on stage

choices.label: A. When a ball rolls down a hill, its potential energy converts into kinetic energy — the total energy stays the same
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ This is the Law of Conservation of Energy! At the top of the hill, the ball has maximum potential energy (stored energy due to height) and zero kinetic energy (energy of motion). As it rolls down, potential energy converts to kinetic energy — the ball speeds up. At the bottom, kinetic energy is maximum. The total energy (PE + KE) stays constant (minus a little lost to friction as heat).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. A ball rolling on a flat surface has both high potential energy and high kinetic energy
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 On a flat surface (at ground level), the ball has very little potential energy because PE depends on HEIGHT. It has kinetic energy (it is moving), but not potential energy. Potential energy increases with height — a ball on top of a hill has high PE, a ball at the bottom has low PE. A rolling ball on flat ground is almost all kinetic energy.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Machines create new energy, which is why they can do work that humans cannot
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Machines NEVER create new energy — the Law of Conservation of Energy says energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another. A car engine converts chemical energy (fuel) into kinetic energy (motion). Machines are powerful because they convert energy efficiently and can apply forces humans cannot, but the energy always comes from somewhere!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Friction destroys energy completely — the energy just disappears
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Friction does not DESTROY energy — it CONVERTS kinetic energy into heat energy. Rub your hands together — they get warm! That warmth IS the kinetic energy transformed into heat by friction. Car brakes convert motion energy into heat (they get very hot!). The energy is still there, just in a form that is harder to use for motion.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

glossary_terms.definition: A push or pull that can change an object's speed, direction, or shape. Forces are measured in Newtons (N) and always act in a specific direction.
The force that pulls all objects toward the center of the Earth (or any massive body). On Earth's surface, gravity accelerates all objects at 9.8 m/s squared.
A force that opposes the motion of surfaces sliding against each other. Friction depends on the roughness of surfaces and the force pressing them together.
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant speed, unless acted upon by an unbalanced force. Also called the Law of Inertia.
Force equals mass times acceleration (F = m x a). The more force you apply, the more an object accelerates. Heavier objects need more force to accelerate.
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force.
A simple machine consisting of a rigid bar that pivots on a fixed point (fulcrum). Levers multiply force — the longer the lever arm, the less force needed.
A simple machine using a wheel and rope to change the direction of a force. Compound pulleys (multiple wheels) can multiply force at the cost of distance.
A flat surface tilted at an angle (a ramp). It reduces the force needed to raise objects by increasing the distance over which the force is applied.
A type of friction that acts on objects moving through air. It depends on the object's speed, shape, and surface area. Also called drag.
The factor by which a simple machine multiplies force. A machine with MA of 3 lets you lift 30N with only 10N of effort (but you push 3 times the distance).
The rate at which an object's speed changes. Measured in meters per second squared (m/s squared). Positive acceleration means speeding up; negative means slowing down.

endings.title: Master Engineer
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Forces & Motion Park! Your understanding of physics is extraordinary, your safety record is impeccable, and your Rube Goldberg machine has inspired the entire school. Coach Newton nominates you for the District Science Award, and the local newspaper features your Physics Showcase project on the front page. You have proven that curiosity, hard work, and engineering creativity can move the world!

endings.title: Skilled Physics Builder
endings.message: You have become a skilled physics builder with solid knowledge and good workshop practices! Your Physics Showcase project demonstrates real competence in understanding forces and building machines. Coach Newton is proud of your progress and says you are ready for the advanced engineering elective next year. Your skills are genuine and your future in science is bright!

endings.title: Workshop Regular
endings.message: You completed the Forces & Motion Park program with mixed results. Some weeks were great and others were tough, but you stuck with it and learned the basics of forces and simple machines. Coach Newton says there is always next semester to improve, and the foundation you built will serve you well. Keep building — every expert was once a beginner!

endings.title: Struggling Student
endings.message: The Forces & Motion Park was a tough journey for you. Many of the physics concepts were confusing, and the builds did not always go as planned. But here is the important thing — you did not give up. Coach Newton arranges extra tutoring sessions for you and says: 'The students who struggle the most often end up understanding the deepest, because they had to fight for every insight.' Your story is not over!

endings.title: Workshop Probation
endings.message: Due to repeated safety violations — dropping heavy objects carelessly, launching projectiles without clearance, and ignoring goggles rules — Coach Newton has placed you on Workshop Probation. You can only observe experiments until you pass the safety certification test. Gizmo has volunteered to tutor you personally. Safety around heavy, fast-moving objects is non-negotiable. This setback is temporary — learn from it and come back stronger!

reflection_prompt: Which lever, if you'd moved it earlier, would have changed your outcome the most?
